did_you_know.text: Did you know? Ecclesiastes describes the oppressed as suffering from tears and having no one to comfort them, while their oppressors have power on their side.

Did you know? Ecclesiastes takes an extreme view of suffering: he considers those who have not yet been born better off than the living or the dead, because they have not seen the evil done under the sun.
Did you know? According to Ecclesiastes, hard work and skill can provoke envy among people; therefore, even personal success may prove to be futile and chasing the wind.
Did you know? Ecclesiastes prefers “one handful with peace and quiet” over “two handfuls with hard work and chasing the wind.”
Did you know? Ecclesiastes criticizes a person who works endlessly and accumulates wealth without ever being satisfied, not knowing for whom he is laboring while denying himself enjoyment.
Did you know? The chapter explicitly affirms the value of partnership: two people receive a better return for their work because they can benefit from helping each other.
Did you know? The image of “a cord of three strands” emphasizes the strength of partnership: two can stand together against an attacker, and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
Did you know? Ecclesiastes places a poor but wise child above an old and foolish king, teaching that status and age do not guarantee wisdom or leadership ability.

Did you know? Even when a new generation wins the people’s support and replaces its predecessor, Ecclesiastes warns that this is no guarantee of happiness; the hopes of future generations may also prove futile.
